# Chinese junk and Zheng He's treasure fleets (`chinese_junk_treasure_ships`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/navigation.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Navigation, transport & exploration (`navigation`)
- Deps: helped by watertight_bulkheads, ship_design_caravel_carrack
- Core idea: The Chinese junk had flat transverse bulkheads that divide the hull into watertight compartments, a large stern rudder that can be raised in shallow water, and sails stiffened with bamboo battens that are reefed in seconds by lowering them, hold their shape upwind and survive tears. With such ships Zheng He led seven voyages (1405–1433) with up to some 250–300 vessels and about 27,000 men to India, Arabia and East Africa, decades before the Portuguese reached India; the Ming court then stopped them and restricted private sea trade.
- Pitfalls:
  - Repeating the 120–135 m length for the largest treasure ships as fact; the large dimensions come from texts of disputed reliability, and smaller modern reconstructions are estimates too
  - Repeating Gavin Menzies' claim that the Chinese reached America in 1421; it has no evidence
  - Thinking junks were primitive; in 1490 they were in several ways ahead of European ships
- History: china: Tang – compartmented boats (Rugao find); c. 1277 Quanzhou wreck with 13 compartments; 1405–1433 Zheng He's voyages; from 1371 and again after 1433 Ming maritime prohibitions; europe: c. 1298 – Marco Polo describes compartmented Chinese ships
- Read:
  - Sally K. Church, Zheng He: An Investigation into the Plausibility of 450-ft Treasure Ships, Monumenta Serica 53 (2005), 1–43
  - Ma Huan, Ying-yai Sheng-lan: The Overall Survey of the Ocean's Shores (tr. J. V. G. Mills, 1970)
  - Edward L. Dreyer, Zheng He: China and the Oceans in the Early Ming Dynasty, 1405–1433 (2007)
  - Joseph Needham, Science and Civilisation in China, vol. 4 part 3: Civil Engineering and Nautics (1971)
